etymologies.etymologyHTML: From earlier mingil, mengle, from Middle English menglen, equivalent to ming +‎ -le. Cognate with Dutch mengen (“to mingle, mix”), German mengen (“to mingle, mix”). More at ming.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To intermix; to combine or join, as an individual or part, with other parts, but commonly so as to be distinguishable in the product.[1]

quote.citation: 1530 January 27 (Gregorian calendar), W[illiam] T[yndale], transl., [The Pentateuch] (Tyndale Bible), Malborow [Marburg], Hesse:  […]  Hans Luft [actually Antwerp: Johan Hoochstraten], →OCLC, Exodus ix:[24], folio XV, verso:
quote.text: [T]here was hayle ãd fyre mẽgled with the hayle,  […]

quote.citation: 1838, Martin Farquhar Tupper, “Of Searching for Pride”, in Proverbial Philosophy: A Book of Thoughts and Arguments, Originally Treated, London: Joseph Rickerby, […], →OCLC, page 69:
quote.text: Be aware of the smiling enemy, that openly sheatheth his weapon, / But mingleth poison in secret with the sacred salt of hospitality.

quote.citation: 2006 September 11, Sheryl Gay Stolberg, “Bush Mourns 9/11 at Ground Zero as N.Y. Remembers”, in The New York Times‎[1], New York, N.Y.: The New York Times Company, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2011-09-26:
quote.text: Across the city yesterday, there was a feeling of bittersweet reunion as streams of humanity converged and mingled at dozens of memorial services.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To associate or unite in a figurative way, or by ties of relationship.
To cause or allow to intermarry.

quote.citation: 1535 October 14 (Gregorian calendar), Myles Coverdale, transl., Biblia: The Byble, […] (Coverdale Bible), [Cologne or Marburg]: [Eucharius Cervicornus and Johannes Soter?], →OCLC, III. Essdras [1 Esdras] viij:[87], folio vij, verso, column 2:
quote.text: [W]e haue bꝛokẽ thy ſtatutes ⁊ cõmaundementes agayne, ⁊ mengled oꝛ ſelues wt the vnclẽnes of the outlandiſh heithen.[W]e have broken thy statutes and commandments again, and mingled ourselves with the uncleanness of the foreign heathen.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Ezra 9:2, column 1:
quote.text: [T]he holy ſeed haue mingled themſelues with the people of thoſe lands,  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To deprive of purity by mixture; to contaminate.[1]

quote.citation: a. 1729, John Rogers, The Necessity of Universal Obedience:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make or prepare by mixing the ingredients of.[1]

quote.citation: 1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne, “The Interview”, in The Scarlet Letter, a Romance, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, →OCLC, page 86:
quote.text: The physician  […]  proceeded to mingle another draught.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To put together; to join.[1]

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene vi], page 375, column 2:
quote.text: Some dozen Romanes of vs, and your Lord (The beſt Feather of our wing) haue mingled ſummes To buy a Preſent for the Emperor:  […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To socialize with different people at a social event.

quote.citation: 2009, Jane Buckingham, The Modern Girl's Guide to Life:
quote.text: And allow a bit of a cocktail hour before the meal so that when your guests arrive, you have time to mingle before you step into the kitchen.

definitions.definition: The act of informally meeting numerous people in a group

quote.citation: 2019, Sally Lou Oaks Loveman, Speak: Love Your Story, Your Audience Is Waiting:
quote.text: When speakers engage their audiences before they speak with a quick mingle and keep the engagement going throughout the speech, the access point for fear is cut off because there is no silence.
